title: DOL Proposes Raising H-1B Prevailing Wages by Up to 33%, Threatening Employer Sponsorship Economics
excerpt: A proposed rule would shift wage floors to higher percentiles across all four levels, adding an estimated $14,000 per worker annually and potentially pricing some employers out of the visa program.
body:
• The U.S. Department of Labor proposed raising all four prevailing wage levels to higher percentiles: Level I from the 17th to the 34th percentile (a 33.4% increase), with similar jumps across Levels II through IV.
  • The rule would apply to H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM labor certification programs, affecting the largest foreign-worker visa categories in the U.S.
  • The DOL estimates the changes would increase average certified wages by approximately $14,000 per worker per year.
  • The comment period closed May 26, 2026, and the rule could take effect in the coming months.

What the Rule Proposes

On March 26, 2026, the U.S. Department of Labor published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would overhaul how prevailing wages are calculated for several employment-based visa programs. The proposed rule shifts wage floors from their current Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) percentiles to substantially higher thresholds.

The specific changes:

  • Level I (Entry): From approximately the 17th percentile to the 34th — a 33.4% increase
  • Level II: From the 34th to the 52nd percentile — a 24.5% increase
  • Level III: From the 50th to the 70th percentile — a 20.8% increase
  • Level IV (Senior): From the 67th to the 88th percentile — a 21.7% increase

The rule cites Presidential Proclamation No. 10973, issued in September 2025, which directed the secretary of labor to revise prevailing wage levels under the H-1B program. The DOL argues that current methodology allows employers to pay foreign nationals "significantly less" than what similarly qualified U.S. workers earn for the same jobs.

Who Gets Hit

H-1B employers would constitute the largest affected group by far. The rule also covers H-1B1 employers sponsoring nationals of Chile and Singapore, E-3 employers sponsoring Australian nationals, and employers pursuing PERM labor certification for EB-2 and EB-3 employment-based green cards.

The impact falls hardest on entry-level and mid-level positions. A Level I software developer in the San Francisco metro area, for instance, could see their required minimum wage jump by tens of thousands of dollars. For employers already operating on thin margins or sponsoring workers in cost-sensitive roles, the economics of H-1B sponsorship could become prohibitive.

"It is an earthquake for the H-1B program right now. Employers looking to renew H-1B visas for workers could see a $30,000 to $40,000 increase in those workers' wages. They cannot afford that."

— Nandini Nair, Immigration Partner, Greenspoon Marder LLP

Impact on Indian IT Workers

Indian nationals hold the overwhelming majority of H-1B visas, and the proposed wage increases would directly affect their employment prospects. Major Indian IT services firms — historically the largest H-1B sponsors — already faced pressure from the new wage-weighted lottery system that favors higher-paying positions. This rule would compound that pressure by raising the floor for all wage levels.

For individual H-1B holders seeking to renew visas, the rule creates uncertainty. Employers may need to either raise salaries substantially to meet new thresholds or decline to sponsor renewals, potentially forcing workers into status gaps or departure from the U.S.

PERM labor certification applications would also be affected, meaning the green card process for many Indian workers in the decade-long EB-2 and EB-3 queues could face additional employer cost hurdles.

What Employers Should Do Now

Immigration attorneys are advising employers to begin reviewing compensation structures for all foreign-worker positions. The proposed rule would not apply retroactively — existing LCAs and prevailing wage determinations would be grandfathered. But new applications filed after the effective date would face the higher thresholds.

The DOL has preserved the option for employers to use private wage surveys as an alternative to OEWS-based prevailing wages, though the agency indicated it intends to monitor their use to prevent abuse.

FY2027 H-1B cap petitions, which had to be filed by June 30, 2026, are expected to remain unaffected since their LCAs were filed before the rule's anticipated effective date. But renewals and transfers filed afterward will face the new wage floors.
